title: A robust and modular cesium magneto-optical trap using diverging laser beams
authors: Paola Luna, Kenneth Nakasone, Andrei Zhukov, Philip Wondrak, Brian P. Anderson, Benjamin F. Kanzer, Cristian D. Panda
abstract: Magneto-optical traps (MOTs) are a workhorse technology for neutral-atom quantum sensing, simulation, and computing. Here, we demonstrate a MOT optimized for inertial quantum sensing and precision metrology applications. Our MOT traps $4\times10^8$ cesium (Cs) atoms in a robust, modular system that achieves stable operation through two design features: (1) we use diverging cooling laser beams to reduce unwanted reflections and (2) optical elements are mounted in a fiber-coupled, compact, and modular cage rigidly attached to the vacuum chamber. Following polarization-gradient cooling (PGC), the system produces atom samples with temperatures below 10 $μ$K, similar to those achieved in conventional MOTs that use collimated laser beams. In addition, we observe trapping of $2\times10^7$ Cs atoms in a non-conventional MOT geometry, where the cooling laser beams are diagonal to the principal axis of the quadrupole magnetic field.
summary: The authors present an advanced, modular Magneto-Optical Trap (MOT) designed specifically for high-precision quantum sensing using cesium atoms. By implementing diverging laser beams and a compact optical cage system, they achieve stable trapping of millions of atoms at temperatures below $10 \mu	ext{K}$. This demonstrates a significant engineering improvement over conventional MOTs, enhancing reliability for future quantum applications.
main_problem: To develop a robust, modular Magneto-Optical Trap (MOT) optimized for high-precision quantum sensing and metrology applications.
main_result: The developed MOT successfully traps large numbers of cesium atoms ($\sim 4	imes10^8$) with low temperatures ($<10 \mu	ext{K}$) while maintaining long-term stability, even when using novel diverging laser beam geometries.
method: The system employs a modular optical cage setup and utilizes diverging cooling laser beams instead of conventional collimated beams to improve robustness against reflections. Cooling is optimized via Polarization-Gradient Cooling (PGC).
model_or_system: The physical platform is a Cesium Magneto-Optical Trap (MOT) adapted for stability and modularity. It can operate in standard or non-conventional diagonal magnetic field geometries.
key_observables: Atom number ($	ext{Cs}$ atoms), temperature ($T$), spatial widths ($\sigma_{X'}, \sigma_{Z'}$), and long-term stability over $>50$ hours.
important_parameters: Optimal MOT parameters include gradients near $6 	ext{ G/cm}$, intensity $\sim 1.1 	ext{ mW/cm}^2$, and detuning at $2\pi 	imes 12 	ext{ MHz}$. PGC duration is optimized around $6 	ext{ ms}$.
main_assumptions: The accuracy of temperature measurement via Time-of-Flight (TOF) method is limited below $10 \mu	ext{K}$; the diagonal MOT configuration is noted to be highly sensitive to parameter drift.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the overall setup using six optical cages, show temperature measurements via TOF fitting, detail optimization scans for 3D MOT parameters and PGC duration, and track long-term stability over $>52$ hours.
paper_structure: The paper details the motivation (need for robust MOTs), presents the novel diverging beam/modular optical system, optimizes loading and cooling stages (PGC), validates performance through temperature and atom number measurements, and concludes by testing stability in both conventional and non-conventional geometries.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses practical engineering challenges in quantum sensing platforms—namely, mechanical robustness and optical coupling efficiency—by modifying the standard MOT setup. The use of diverging beams is a key technical advance for field deployment.
